1: # LLM Wiki — a second brain for AI agents
2: 
3: Turn PDFs, articles, transcripts, and notes into a shared wiki that your AI agents can search, cite, and keep up to date. Add a source once. Ask questions later. Keep the useful answers.
4: 
5: Works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, OpenClaw, Pi, OMP, and Hermes. [Read the documentation](https://praneybehl.github.io/llm-wiki-plugin/).
6: 
7: ## What is LLM Wiki?
8: 
9: AI agents are good at the task in front of them, but a new session starts with limited context. LLM Wiki gives them a shared memory that can live in one personal wiki across all projects or inside a specific project.
10: 
11: When you add a source, the agent turns it into linked Markdown pages. Later, it can find the right section and answer with citations. Useful answers can be saved back into the wiki, so the knowledge grows instead of being rebuilt from scratch.
12: 
13: Everything canonical stays in readable Markdown. Default semantic search is local—no hosted vector database or embedding service.
14: 
15: ## What's new in v3.2.0
16: 
17: - **Learn from completed work.** `/wiki:learn` captures verified successes/failures and consolidates cited patterns, applicability and counterexamples.
18: - **Turn evidence into tested procedures.** `/wiki:evolve` runs training, evidence consolidation, whole-skill proposals, validation, and independent final testing, retaining rejected attempts. Adapters for nine supported agent hosts provide bounded runs, durable tool traces and cross-agent transfer; see the [execution requirements](https://praneybehl.github.io/llm-wiki-plugin/evolution.html).
19: - **Explicit apply and rollback.** Only a reviewed, passing change can be applied; whole-skill snapshot checks prevent overwriting intervening edits.
20: - **Runnable evaluation examples.** Separate training, validation and final-test tasks cover source-grounded answers and file artifacts, with calibrated judging, paired task-level analysis, and ingestion/graph/hybrid-search checks. Fictional fixtures stay outside the installed skill.
21: - **Compatible upgrade.** Existing Markdown and commands remain valid. `/wiki:upgrade` adds optional templates and archive guidance idempotently.
22: 
23: See [Learning and skill evolution](https://praneybehl.github.io/llm-wiki-plugin/evolution.html) for the full workflow, evaluation limits and inference costs. This release adds tooling; it does not claim measured model gains.
24: 
25: The evolution workflow adapts [WikiSkill: Compiling Agent Experience into Persistent Knowledge for Skill Evolution](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.27454v1) (Google Research and Virginia Tech, 2026): persistent experience-to-pattern learning, repeated skill proposals, retained failures, validation-only selection and independent final testing. See [what we adapted and changed](docs/evolution.md#research-basis-and-adaptation) and the [measured results](eval/evolution/workflows/README.md). Our study rejected both proposals; no quality improvement was demonstrated.
26: 
27: ## Why use it?
28: 
29: - **Stop repeating project context.** Your agent can read the knowledge you already collected.
30: - **Use the same wiki across agents.** The files are plain Markdown, not tied to one model or tool.
31: - **Trace every answer.** Citations point back to the wiki page and original source.
32: - **Keep the wiki healthy.** The agent updates links, summaries, and contradictions as new sources arrive.
33: - **Stay in control.** Your pages remain readable, editable, and versionable.
34: 
35: LLM Wiki works best for knowledge that grows over time: research, meeting notes, customer calls, papers, articles, and project decisions. Use a regular database when your main problem is structured records and transactions.
36: 
37: ## Installation
38: `uv` is the only prerequisite: it creates the pinned script environments on every supported platform. Install it using the [official uv instructions](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) before running `/wiki:init` or the natural-language equivalent.
39: 
40: Plugin/skill installation copies all agent-facing commands and bundled tools. Wiki initialization then performs mandatory runtime setup: FastEmbed `0.8.0`, sqlite-vec `0.1.9`, PyYAML `6.0.3`, the local `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5` model, the parse cache, and vectors for every existing section. Upgrade runs the same setup again, incrementally synchronizing changed and deleted sections.
41: 
42: 
43: ### Claude Code — full plugin
44: 
45: The native path: the skill, the nine `/wiki:*` slash commands, and the marketplace manifest all ship in one install.
46: 
47: ```
48: /plugin marketplace add praneybehl/llm-wiki-plugin
49: /plugin install llm-wiki@llm-wiki
50: ```
51: 
52: Once installed, the plugin works in any project. Installation does not decide where your wiki lives.
53: 
54: ### Other coding agents — skill only
55: 
56: The `llm-wiki` skill uses the standard [agentskills.io](https://agentskills.io) format, so it installs cleanly into any agent supported by the [`skills` CLI](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills). Pick the `--agent` flag that matches your setup:
57: 
58: ```bash
59: # Install globally so the skill is available across all projects
60: npx skills add praneybehl/llm-wiki-plugin -a <agent> -g
61: 
62: # Or install into the current project only
63: npx skills add praneybehl/llm-wiki-plugin -a <agent>
64: ```
65: 
66: | Agent | `--agent` value | Invoke via | Scripts run |
67: |-------|-----------------|------------|:-----------:|
68: | Claude Code | `claude-code` | `/wiki:*` slash commands (bundled) or natural language | ✅ |
69: | Codex (OpenAI) | `codex` | `/skills` or `$llm-wiki` / natural language | ✅ |
70: | Cursor | `cursor` | `/llm-wiki` or natural language | ✅ |
71: | Gemini CLI | `gemini-cli` | `/skills` management commands / natural language | ✅ |
72: | OpenCode | `opencode` | natural language (agent invokes the native `skill` tool) | ✅ |
73: | OpenClaw | `openclaw` | auto-exposed as a user command | ✅ |
74: | Pi Agent | `pi` | `/skill:llm-wiki` or natural language | ✅ |
75: | OMP ("Oh My Pi") | manual (see below) | natural language (skills auto-surface via `skill://`) | ✅ |
76: 
77: OpenCode also reads `.claude/skills/` and `~/.claude/skills/`, so if you already installed the skill for Claude Code you can use it in OpenCode without a second install.
78: 
79: **Hermes Agent** (Nous Research), **OMP** ("Oh My Pi"), and other agentskills.io-compatible runtimes that aren't yet in the `npx skills` registry can still use this skill — clone the repo and symlink or copy `skills/llm-wiki/` into the agent's skills directory. Hermes reads from `~/.hermes/skills/`; OMP reads managed/user skills from `~/.omp/agent/skills/` and surfaces them via `skill://`.
80: 
81: ```bash
82: git clone https://github.com/praneybehl/llm-wiki-plugin.git
83: mkdir -p ~/.hermes/skills ~/.omp/agent/skills
84: ln -s "$(pwd)/llm-wiki-plugin/skills/llm-wiki" ~/.hermes/skills/llm-wiki
85: ln -s "$(pwd)/llm-wiki-plugin/skills/llm-wiki" ~/.omp/agent/skills/llm-wiki
86: ```
87: 
88: A few things to know when using the skill outside Claude Code:
89: 
90: - **Slash commands are Claude Code-only.** The nine `/wiki:*` commands live in `commands/wiki/` as Claude Code plugin manifests. In other agents, invoke the skill by natural language ("add this paper to the wiki", "what does the wiki say about X", "lint the wiki") — the SKILL.md handles the rest.
91: - **All bundled tools are agent-accessible.** Every listed agent can invoke `setup_wiki.py`, hybrid/lexical search, lint, stats, graph lint/extract/query, and initialization through the installed skill. Dependency-bearing scripts carry pinned PEP 723 metadata and run with `uv run --script`; initialization and upgrade verify the full runtime before reporting readiness.
92: - **The wiki itself is agent-agnostic.** It's just a directory of markdown files. You can ingest with one agent and query with another; nothing in `wiki/` ties it to a specific runtime.
93: 
94: ### Choose where the wiki lives
95: 
96: Skill scope and wiki scope are separate choices. A global skill install makes the skill available in every project; it does not create or select a global wiki.
97: 
98: - **One personal wiki across projects:** keep it at a stable user-level path such as `~/wiki/`, keep raw sources under `~/wiki/raw/`, and point your agent's global instructions there. Work from any project can then be deliberately ingested into the same wiki.
99: - **One wiki for a project:** keep `wiki/` and `raw/` in the project and point the project's agent-memory file to them. Choose this when the knowledge should be isolated or versioned with that repository.
100: 
101: A global wiki does not automatically crawl or ingest every project. The agent adds project facts, decisions, and source material when you ask it to ingest them or when your global instructions explicitly tell it to preserve durable findings.
102: 
103: ## Quick start
104: 
105: For one personal wiki shared across projects:
106: 
107: ```
108: /wiki:init --global
109: ```
110: 
111: This initializes `~/wiki/` with raw sources under `~/wiki/raw/` and proposes a matching stanza for your agent's global instructions.
112: 
113: For a wiki isolated to the current project:
114: 
115: ```
116: /wiki:init
117: ```
118: 
119: Already have a wiki from an earlier plugin version? Run `/wiki:upgrade` instead. Init and upgrade both install and verify the complete pinned local runtime, cache the embedding model, build the parse cache, and synchronize all current vectors. They add missing wiki files idempotently and never overwrite existing pages or `SCHEMA.md`.
120: 
121: Initialization bootstraps the selected wiki and raw-source roots with `SCHEMA.md`, `index.md`, `log.md`, and a page template, then emits a JSON runtime report. Setup is complete only when it reports `"status": "ready"`.
122: 
123: As part of the same step, the skill proposes a location pointer so the agent remembers the wiki in future sessions: global instructions for a personal global wiki, or the project's agent-memory file for a project wiki. The skill never writes to a memory file without your approval; see `skills/llm-wiki/references/agent-memory-integration.md` for both variants.
124: 
125: Drop your first source into the configured raw root (for example `~/wiki/raw/` in the global layout), then:
126: 
127: ```
128: /wiki:ingest ~/wiki/raw/your-source.pdf
129: ```
130: 
131: Claude reads the source (chunk-reading if it's large), discusses the takeaways with you, writes a summary page, identifies which existing entity and concept pages it touches, surgically updates them with `str_replace`, creates new pages for new entities and concepts (each with at least one inbound link), updates the index, and appends to the log.
132: 
133: Once you have a few sources in:
134: 
135: ```
136: /wiki:query What does my wiki say about X?
137: ```
138: 
139: Claude reads the index to find candidate pages, reads them, synthesizes an answer with `[[wikilink]]` citations, and offers to file substantive answers back into `wiki/synthesis/` so the exploration compounds.
140: 
141: Periodically, run a health check:
142: 
143: ```
144: /wiki:lint
145: ```
146: 
147: This catches orphan pages, broken wikilinks, oversized pages, missing frontmatter, and stale claims. Findings are presented as proposed edits — Claude doesn't rewrite your wiki silently.
148: 
149: ## Commands
150: 
151: | Command | What it does |
152: |---------|--------------|
153: | `/wiki:init [--global]` | Bootstrap a personal global wiki or a wiki in the current project (both include the graph layer). |
154: | `/wiki:ingest <source>` | Process a new source into the wiki; refreshes the graph layer when present. |
155: | `/wiki:query <question>` | Answer a question from the wiki with citations; consults `graph.sqlite` for relational questions when available. |
156: | `/wiki:lint` | Structural and semantic health check; also runs graph lint when `wiki/graph/ontology.yaml` exists. |
157: | `/wiki:stats` | Show wiki size, link density, and which scaling threshold the wiki is at. |
158: | `/wiki:graph <action>` | `extract` / `lint` / `neighbors` / `edges` / `path` / `facts` against the compiled graph layer. |
159: | `/wiki:learn <task artifacts>` | Capture verified experience and consolidate reusable, evidence-linked patterns. |
160: | `/wiki:evolve <goal or action>` | Propose, evaluate, inspect, apply or roll back a skill improvement; retain all trial results. |
161: | `/wiki:upgrade` | Upgrade an existing wiki to the current plugin version (idempotent file ops + walked SCHEMA.md merge). |
162: 
163: You don't have to use the commands — Claude triggers the underlying skill on natural-language requests too ("add this paper to my wiki", "what does the wiki say about diffusion", "lint the wiki"). The commands are there when you want explicit invocation.
164: 
165: ## Architecture
166: 
167: The wiki has three layers and three operations.
168: 
169: **The three layers** are *raw sources* (your immutable source material in `raw/`), *the wiki* (LLM-owned markdown pages in `wiki/`, organized into `sources/`, `entities/`, `concepts/`, `synthesis/`), and *the schema* (`wiki/SCHEMA.md`, the configuration file that documents the conventions for this specific wiki and that you co-evolve with Claude over time).
170: 
171: **The three operations** are *ingest* (compile a new source into the wiki, touching ten or fifteen pages in one pass), *query* (navigate the wiki to answer a question, with the option to file the answer back as a new synthesis page), and *lint* (periodic health check on structural and semantic integrity).
172: 
173: There is also an **optional fourth layer**: the graph at `wiki/graph/`. Pages can declare typed `graph:` metadata in frontmatter (e.g. `founded`, `proposed`, `depends_on`) with an explicit source-page slug and evidence quote. A bundled extractor compiles every page into `nodes.jsonl`, `edges.jsonl`, `graph.sqlite`, and `graph.graphml`. **Markdown stays canonical** — the graph can be deleted and rebuilt at any time. Use `/wiki:graph` for relational queries that the index alone can't answer cheaply ("what's connected to X", "who proposed Y", "shortest path A → B").
174: 
175: For the full architecture write-up including page types, frontmatter conventions, the rationale behind each design choice, and the workflow procedures, see the reference docs inside the skill at `skills/llm-wiki/references/`. The graph layer is documented in `skills/llm-wiki/references/graph-workflow.md`.
176: 
177: ## Learning from experience
178: 
179: The optional evolution workflow connects immutable task evidence to ordinary source/concept patterns, then to measured skill changes. Candidate skills are isolated during evaluation. The durable `.evolution/` archive is excluded from normal wiki retrieval; cited lessons and summaries remain searchable. Use `wiki_evolve.py --help` or the [agent workflow](skills/llm-wiki/references/evolution-workflow.md). Model runners may incur remote inference costs; capture and the harness itself are stdlib-only.
180: 
181: ## How it scales
182: 
183: The single biggest failure mode of the LLM Wiki pattern is the wiki becoming a context bottleneck as it grows. The plugin's design is shaped largely around avoiding that failure.
184: 
185: **Atomic pages.** Every page is about one concept. Soft cap 400 lines, hard cap 800 lines. The lint script enforces this. Any single page read is bounded, so even at a thousand pages a query that reads five pages stays well within context.
186: 
187: **Sharded indexes.** When `wiki/index.md` exceeds 300 lines or the wiki passes ~150 pages, the index shards into per-type files under `wiki/indexes/`. The top-level index becomes a tiny directory of shards. Reading the index is now a two-step lookup but each step is bounded.
188: 
189: **YAML frontmatter on every page.** The `wiki_search.py` script can filter on `type`, `tags`, and `updated` without reading page bodies, so retrieval scales independently of total wiki size.
190: 
191: **Index-first navigation.** Queries read the index first, identify candidate pages from one-line summaries, and only read those. The index is the cache that makes the whole pattern scalable.
192: 
193: **Local hybrid search.** When index summaries are insufficient, `uv run --script skills/llm-wiki/scripts/wiki_search.py "query terms"` ranks Markdown sections with local FastEmbed semantic vectors plus BM25, fused through RRF. sqlite-vec stores content-hashed vectors in `wiki/.wiki-cache/embeddings.sqlite`; only changed sections are re-embedded. No API key, provider, or outbound wiki/query text is involved. `--json` emits evidence rows and `--cache` persists parsed sections. For the genuinely dependency-free path, invoke `python skills/llm-wiki/scripts/wiki_search.py "query terms" --no-embed`; `--granularity page` restores whole-page ranking.
194: 
195: **Surgical edits.** When updating a page during ingest, Claude uses `str_replace` to touch the relevant section, not rewrite the page. Fast, token-efficient, and preserves diff quality if you keep the wiki in git.
196: 
197: **Chunked source ingestion.** Large raw sources (long PDFs, multi-hour transcripts) are read in chunks during ingest, not loaded whole. The ingest workflow handles this automatically.
198: 
199: The `/wiki:stats` command surfaces which threshold you're at and what migration to do next. The full scaling playbook with thresholds and migration procedures is at `skills/llm-wiki/references/scaling-playbook.md`.
200: 
201: ## What it doesn't try to be
202: 
203: This is a markdown-based personal knowledge base, not a database. If your domain is fundamentally relational — tracking 100,000 customer records, complex org structures, financial ledgers with strict referential integrity — a real database serves better. Markdown plus grep plus frontmatter scales further than people expect (Karpathy's own wiki was about 100 articles and 400K words working fine), but at some point the right tool changes.
204: 
205: Failure modes to know about, all discussed in `skills/llm-wiki/SKILL.md`: silent corruption (a misreading of one source becomes an authoritative-looking wiki page that influences subsequent ingests — mitigated by mandatory `sources:` frontmatter and lint), the wiki-reads-its-own-output drift (Claude treating prior wiki pages as ground truth rather than checking against raw sources — mitigated by the ingest workflow's instruction to re-read raw sources when updating claims), and the maintenance ratchet (lint reports growing faster than you can review — mitigated by the scalability discipline, but if it happens, the schema needs revision).
206: 
207: ## Integrations
208: 
209: The skill is the **agent-side** install — every adapter table above gets you that. For specific platforms there's also an optional **human-side** companion that brings the wiki into view where operators already work.
210: 
211: ### Paperclip — `paperclip-plugin-llm-wiki`
212: 
213: For teams that run their work in [Paperclip](https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip), an optional plugin at [`integrations/paperclip/plugin/`](./integrations/paperclip/plugin/) surfaces the wiki inside Paperclip's UI. Five surfaces, all read-only:
214: 
215: | Surface | What it does |
216: |---|---|
217: | Wiki sidebar | Browse the wiki by type, drill into pages, search across the whole wiki |
218: | Full-page view | The same browser at full width — for reading multiple linked pages |
219: | Issue context tab | Top wiki pages relevant to the open issue, ranked by BM25 over title + description |
220: | Dashboard health widget | Page count, lint status (pass / warn / fail), link density, sharding-threshold messages |
221: | `wiki.query` agent tool | BM25 search via tool call — for HTTP-only adapters that don't run the skill directly |
222: 
223: Install the companion:
224: 
225: ```bash
226: pnpm paperclipai plugin install paperclip-plugin-llm-wiki
227: ```
228: 
229: The plugin is **read-only by design** and pairs with the skill. The skill writes the wiki on heartbeat; the plugin reads it from inside Paperclip. Editing still happens through agents on heartbeat or the operator's editor of choice (Obsidian, Claude Code, direct SSH).
230: 
231: Documentation:
232: 
233: - [`integrations/paperclip/plugin/README.md`](./integrations/paperclip/plugin/README.md) — the comprehensive user guide. Install walkthrough, per-surface usage guide, configuration reference, agent-tool JSON shape, security and privacy notes, troubleshooting, FAQ.
234: - [`integrations/paperclip/README.md`](./integrations/paperclip/README.md) — operator-facing decision page. When to install plugin vs. just the skill, first-time setup walkthrough, multi-Company guidance.
235: - [`integrations/paperclip/SPEC.md`](./integrations/paperclip/SPEC.md) — v0.1 design with verbatim references to the live Paperclip plugin SDK source.
236: - [`integrations/paperclip/FEASIBILITY.md`](./integrations/paperclip/FEASIBILITY.md) — Phase 0 validation report; documents the SPEC errata that surfaced against the SDK at `paperclipai/paperclip@master`.
237: 
238: ## Tooling
239: 
240: Once the wiki is set up, you can read and edit pages with any markdown viewer. [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md) is a particularly good fit because of its graph view, `[[wikilinks]]` syntax, and Web Clipper extension, but it isn't required — the wiki is just a directory of markdown files in your project.
241: 
242: The tools require Python 3.10+ and `uv`. Initialization and upgrade invoke `setup_wiki.py`, whose PEP 723 environment pins FastEmbed 0.8.0, sqlite-vec 0.1.9, and PyYAML 6.0.3; it caches the model and synchronizes the complete wiki index. Search, graph lint, and graph extraction also carry their own pinned script metadata. Lexical `wiki_search.py --no-embed`, `wiki_lint.py`, `wiki_stats.py`, and graph queries remain directly runnable with stdlib Python. The bundled scripts live in `skills/llm-wiki/scripts/` after install.
243: 
244: ## Credits
245: 
246: The optional skill-evolution workflow is adapted from the [WikiSkill paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.27454v1). The [adaptation map](docs/evolution.md#research-basis-and-adaptation) distinguishes the research ideas, our implementation choices and validation limits.
247: 
248: The pattern is from Andrej Karpathy's [llm-wiki gist](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f), April 2026. This plugin is one implementation of the pattern; others worth looking at include [vanillaflava/llm-wiki-claude-skills](https://github.com/vanillaflava/llm-wiki-claude-skills), [skyllwt/OmegaWiki](https://github.com/skyllwt/OmegaWiki), and [axoviq-ai/synthadoc](https://github.com/axoviq-ai/synthadoc).
249: 
250: The v2 retrieval architecture was informed by Cerebras's engineering article, [How We Built Our Knowledge Base](https://www.cerebras.ai/blog/how-we-built-our-knowledge-base), especially its section-level retrieval, multi-retriever fusion, evidence packaging, and evaluation approach.
251: 
252: The v3 local retrieval cutover was evaluated against [Basic Memory](https://github.com/basicmachines-co/basic-memory). LLM Wiki adopts the same local-first shape—FastEmbed, SQLite vector search, and incremental derived indexes—while keeping its existing Markdown schema, typed graph, RRF ranking, and agent-native workflows instead of adding Basic Memory's application and MCP service as a second canonical system.
253: 
254: ## License
255: 
256: MIT — see [LICENSE](./LICENSE).
257: 
258: ## Contributing
259: 
260: Issues and PRs welcome. The skill itself is at `skills/llm-wiki/`; the slash commands at `commands/wiki/`. Before opening a PR, please run the bundled scripts against a small test wiki to verify nothing broke.

(End of file - total 260 lines)
</content>

## Why use it?

LLM Wiki works best for knowledge that grows over time: research, meeting notes, customer calls, papers, articles, and project decisions. Use a regular database when your main problem is structured records and transactions.

## Installation
`uv` is the only prerequisite: it creates the pinned script environments on every supported platform. Install it using the [official uv instructions](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) before running `/wiki:init` or the natural-language equivalent.

Plugin/skill installation copies all agent-facing commands and bundled tools. Wiki initialization then performs mandatory runtime setup: FastEmbed `0.8.0`, sqlite-vec `0.1.9`, PyYAML `6.0.3`, the local `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5` model, the parse cache, and vectors for every existing section. Upgrade runs the same setup again, incrementally synchronizing changed and deleted sections.


### Claude Code — full plugin

The native path: the skill, the nine `/wiki:*` slash commands, and the marketplace manifest all ship in one install.

```
/plugin marketplace add praneybehl/llm-wiki-plugin
/plugin install llm-wiki@llm-wiki
```

Once installed, the plugin works in any project. Installation does not decide where your wiki lives.

### Other coding agents — skill only

The `llm-wiki` skill uses the standard [agentskills.io](https://agentskills.io) format, so it installs cleanly into any agent supported by the [`skills` CLI](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills). Pick the `--agent` flag that matches your setup:

```bash
# Install globally so the skill is available across all projects
npx skills add praneybehl/llm-wiki-plugin -a <agent> -g

# Or install into the current project only
npx skills add praneybehl/llm-wiki-plugin -a <agent>
```

| Agent | `--agent` value | Invoke via | Scripts run |
|-------|-----------------|------------|:-----------:|
| Claude Code | `claude-code` | `/wiki:*` slash commands (bundled) or natural language | ✅ |
| Codex (OpenAI) | `codex` | `/skills` or `$llm-wiki` / natural language | ✅ |
| Cursor | `cursor` | `/llm-wiki` or natural language | ✅ |
| Gemini CLI | `gemini-cli` | `/skills` management commands / natural language | ✅ |
| OpenCode | `opencode` | natural language (agent invokes the native `skill` tool) | ✅ |
| OpenClaw | `openclaw` | auto-exposed as a user command | ✅ |
| Pi Agent | `pi` | `/skill:llm-wiki` or natural language | ✅ |
| OMP ("Oh My Pi") | manual (see below) | natural language (skills auto-surface via `skill://`) | ✅ |

OpenCode also reads `.claude/skills/` and `~/.claude/skills/`, so if you already installed the skill for Claude Code you can use it in OpenCode without a second install.

**Hermes Agent** (Nous Research), **OMP** ("Oh My Pi"), and other agentskills.io-compatible runtimes that aren't yet in the `npx skills` registry can still use this skill — clone the repo and symlink or copy `skills/llm-wiki/` into the agent's skills directory. Hermes reads from `~/.hermes/skills/`; OMP reads managed/user skills from `~/.omp/agent/skills/` and surfaces them via `skill://`.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/praneybehl/llm-wiki-plugin.git
mkdir -p ~/.hermes/skills ~/.omp/agent/skills
ln -s "$(pwd)/llm-wiki-plugin/skills/llm-wiki" ~/.hermes/skills/llm-wiki
ln -s "$(pwd)/llm-wiki-plugin/skills/llm-wiki" ~/.omp/agent/skills/llm-wiki
```

A few things to know when using the skill outside Claude Code:

- **Slash commands are Claude Code-only.** The nine `/wiki:*` commands live in `commands/wiki/` as Claude Code plugin manifests. In other agents, invoke the skill by natural language ("add this paper to the wiki", "what does the wiki say about X", "lint the wiki") — the SKILL.md handles the rest.
- **All bundled tools are agent-accessible.** Every listed agent can invoke `setup_wiki.py`, hybrid/lexical search, lint, stats, graph lint/extract/query, and initialization through the installed skill. Dependency-bearing scripts carry pinned PEP 723 metadata and run with `uv run --script`; initialization and upgrade verify the full runtime before reporting readiness.
- **The wiki itself is agent-agnostic.** It's just a directory of markdown files. You can ingest with one agent and query with another; nothing in `wiki/` ties it to a specific runtime.

### Choose where the wiki lives

Skill scope and wiki scope are separate choices. A global skill install makes the skill available in every project; it does not create or select a global wiki.

- **One personal wiki across projects:** keep it at a stable user-level path such as `~/wiki/`, keep raw sources under `~/wiki/raw/`, and point your agent's global instructions there. Work from any project can then be deliberately ingested into the same wiki.
- **One wiki for a project:** keep `wiki/` and `raw/` in the project and point the project's agent-memory file to them. Choose this when the knowledge should be isolated or versioned with that repository.

A global wiki does not automatically crawl or ingest every project. The agent adds project facts, decisions, and source material when you ask it to ingest them or when your global instructions explicitly tell it to preserve durable findings.

## Quick start

For one personal wiki shared across projects:

```
/wiki:init --global
```

This initializes `~/wiki/` with raw sources under `~/wiki/raw/` and proposes a matching stanza for your agent's global instructions.

For a wiki isolated to the current project:

```
/wiki:init
```

Already have a wiki from an earlier plugin version? Run `/wiki:upgrade` instead. Init and upgrade both install and verify the complete pinned local runtime, cache the embedding model, build the parse cache, and synchronize all current vectors. They add missing wiki files idempotently and never overwrite existing pages or `SCHEMA.md`.

Initialization bootstraps the selected wiki and raw-source roots with `SCHEMA.md`, `index.md`, `log.md`, and a page template, then emits a JSON runtime report. Setup is complete only when it reports `"status": "ready"`.

As part of the same step, the skill proposes a location pointer so the agent remembers the wiki in future sessions: global instructions for a personal global wiki, or the project's agent-memory file for a project wiki. The skill never writes to a memory file without your approval; see `skills/llm-wiki/references/agent-memory-integration.md` for both variants.

Drop your first source into the configured raw root (for example `~/wiki/raw/` in the global layout), then:

```
/wiki:ingest ~/wiki/raw/your-source.pdf
```

Claude reads the source (chunk-reading if it's large), discusses the takeaways with you, writes a summary page, identifies which existing entity and concept pages it touches, surgically updates them with `str_replace`, creates new pages for new entities and concepts (each with at least one inbound link), updates the index, and appends to the log.

Once you have a few sources in:

```
/wiki:query What does my wiki say about X?
```

Claude reads the index to find candidate pages, reads them, synthesizes an answer with `[[wikilink]]` citations, and offers to file substantive answers back into `wiki/synthesis/` so the exploration compounds.

Periodically, run a health check:

```
/wiki:lint
```

This catches orphan pages, broken wikilinks, oversized pages, missing frontmatter, and stale claims. Findings are presented as proposed edits — Claude doesn't rewrite your wiki silently.

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `/wiki:init [--global]` | Bootstrap a personal global wiki or a wiki in the current project (both include the graph layer). |
| `/wiki:ingest <source>` | Process a new source into the wiki; refreshes the graph layer when present. |
| `/wiki:query <question>` | Answer a question from the wiki with citations; consults `graph.sqlite` for relational questions when available. |
| `/wiki:lint` | Structural and semantic health check; also runs graph lint when `wiki/graph/ontology.yaml` exists. |
| `/wiki:stats` | Show wiki size, link density, and which scaling threshold the wiki is at. |
| `/wiki:graph <action>` | `extract` / `lint` / `neighbors` / `edges` / `path` / `facts` against the compiled graph layer. |
| `/wiki:learn <task artifacts>` | Capture verified experience and consolidate reusable, evidence-linked patterns. |
| `/wiki:evolve <goal or action>` | Propose, evaluate, inspect, apply or roll back a skill improvement; retain all trial results. |
| `/wiki:upgrade` | Upgrade an existing wiki to the current plugin version (idempotent file ops + walked SCHEMA.md merge). |

You don't have to use the commands — Claude triggers the underlying skill on natural-language requests too ("add this paper to my wiki", "what does the wiki say about diffusion", "lint the wiki"). The commands are there when you want explicit invocation.

## Architecture

The wiki has three layers and three operations.

**The three layers** are *raw sources* (your immutable source material in `raw/`), *the wiki* (LLM-owned markdown pages in `wiki/`, organized into `sources/`, `entities/`, `concepts/`, `synthesis/`), and *the schema* (`wiki/SCHEMA.md`, the configuration file that documents the conventions for this specific wiki and that you co-evolve with Claude over time).

**The three operations** are *ingest* (compile a new source into the wiki, touching ten or fifteen pages in one pass), *query* (navigate the wiki to answer a question, with the option to file the answer back as a new synthesis page), and *lint* (periodic health check on structural and semantic integrity).

There is also an **optional fourth layer**: the graph at `wiki/graph/`. Pages can declare typed `graph:` metadata in frontmatter (e.g. `founded`, `proposed`, `depends_on`) with an explicit source-page slug and evidence quote. A bundled extractor compiles every page into `nodes.jsonl`, `edges.jsonl`, `graph.sqlite`, and `graph.graphml`. **Markdown stays canonical** — the graph can be deleted and rebuilt at any time. Use `/wiki:graph` for relational queries that the index alone can't answer cheaply ("what's connected to X", "who proposed Y", "shortest path A → B").

For the full architecture write-up including page types, frontmatter conventions, the rationale behind each design choice, and the workflow procedures, see the reference docs inside the skill at `skills/llm-wiki/references/`. The graph layer is documented in `skills/llm-wiki/references/graph-workflow.md`.

## Learning from experience

The optional evolution workflow connects immutable task evidence to ordinary source/concept patterns, then to measured skill changes. Candidate skills are isolated during evaluation. The durable `.evolution/` archive is excluded from normal wiki retrieval; cited lessons and summaries remain searchable. Use `wiki_evolve.py --help` or the [agent workflow](skills/llm-wiki/references/evolution-workflow.md). Model runners may incur remote inference costs; capture and the harness itself are stdlib-only.

## How it scales

The single biggest failure mode of the LLM Wiki pattern is the wiki becoming a context bottleneck as it grows. The plugin's design is shaped largely around avoiding that failure.

**Atomic pages.** Every page is about one concept. Soft cap 400 lines, hard cap 800 lines. The lint script enforces this. Any single page read is bounded, so even at a thousand pages a query that reads five pages stays well within context.

**Sharded indexes.** When `wiki/index.md` exceeds 300 lines or the wiki passes ~150 pages, the index shards into per-type files under `wiki/indexes/`. The top-level index becomes a tiny directory of shards. Reading the index is now a two-step lookup but each step is bounded.

**YAML frontmatter on every page.** The `wiki_search.py` script can filter on `type`, `tags`, and `updated` without reading page bodies, so retrieval scales independently of total wiki size.

**Index-first navigation.** Queries read the index first, identify candidate pages from one-line summaries, and only read those. The index is the cache that makes the whole pattern scalable.

**Local hybrid search.** When index summaries are insufficient, `uv run --script skills/llm-wiki/scripts/wiki_search.py "query terms"` ranks Markdown sections with local FastEmbed semantic vectors plus BM25, fused through RRF. sqlite-vec stores content-hashed vectors in `wiki/.wiki-cache/embeddings.sqlite`; only changed sections are re-embedded. No API key, provider, or outbound wiki/query text is involved. `--json` emits evidence rows and `--cache` persists parsed sections. For the genuinely dependency-free path, invoke `python skills/llm-wiki/scripts/wiki_search.py "query terms" --no-embed`; `--granularity page` restores whole-page ranking.

**Surgical edits.** When updating a page during ingest, Claude uses `str_replace` to touch the relevant section, not rewrite the page. Fast, token-efficient, and preserves diff quality if you keep the wiki in git.

**Chunked source ingestion.** Large raw sources (long PDFs, multi-hour transcripts) are read in chunks during ingest, not loaded whole. The ingest workflow handles this automatically.

The `/wiki:stats` command surfaces which threshold you're at and what migration to do next. The full scaling playbook with thresholds and migration procedures is at `skills/llm-wiki/references/scaling-playbook.md`.

## What it doesn't try to be

This is a markdown-based personal knowledge base, not a database. If your domain is fundamentally relational — tracking 100,000 customer records, complex org structures, financial ledgers with strict referential integrity — a real database serves better. Markdown plus grep plus frontmatter scales further than people expect (Karpathy's own wiki was about 100 articles and 400K words working fine), but at some point the right tool changes.

Failure modes to know about, all discussed in `skills/llm-wiki/SKILL.md`: silent corruption (a misreading of one source becomes an authoritative-looking wiki page that influences subsequent ingests — mitigated by mandatory `sources:` frontmatter and lint), the wiki-reads-its-own-output drift (Claude treating prior wiki pages as ground truth rather than checking against raw sources — mitigated by the ingest workflow's instruction to re-read raw sources when updating claims), and the maintenance ratchet (lint reports growing faster than you can review — mitigated by the scalability discipline, but if it happens, the schema needs revision).

## Integrations

The skill is the **agent-side** install — every adapter table above gets you that. For specific platforms there's also an optional **human-side** companion that brings the wiki into view where operators already work.

### Paperclip — `paperclip-plugin-llm-wiki`

For teams that run their work in [Paperclip](https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip), an optional plugin at [`integrations/paperclip/plugin/`](./integrations/paperclip/plugin/) surfaces the wiki inside Paperclip's UI. Five surfaces, all read-only:

| Surface | What it does |
|---|---|
| Wiki sidebar | Browse the wiki by type, drill into pages, search across the whole wiki |
| Full-page view | The same browser at full width — for reading multiple linked pages |
| Issue context tab | Top wiki pages relevant to the open issue, ranked by BM25 over title + description |
| Dashboard health widget | Page count, lint status (pass / warn / fail), link density, sharding-threshold messages |
| `wiki.query` agent tool | BM25 search via tool call — for HTTP-only adapters that don't run the skill directly |

Install the companion:

```bash
pnpm paperclipai plugin install paperclip-plugin-llm-wiki
```

The plugin is **read-only by design** and pairs with the skill. The skill writes the wiki on heartbeat; the plugin reads it from inside Paperclip. Editing still happens through agents on heartbeat or the operator's editor of choice (Obsidian, Claude Code, direct SSH).

Documentation:

- [`integrations/paperclip/plugin/README.md`](./integrations/paperclip/plugin/README.md) — the comprehensive user guide. Install walkthrough, per-surface usage guide, configuration reference, agent-tool JSON shape, security and privacy notes, troubleshooting, FAQ.
- [`integrations/paperclip/README.md`](./integrations/paperclip/README.md) — operator-facing decision page. When to install plugin vs. just the skill, first-time setup walkthrough, multi-Company guidance.
- [`integrations/paperclip/SPEC.md`](./integrations/paperclip/SPEC.md) — v0.1 design with verbatim references to the live Paperclip plugin SDK source.
- [`integrations/paperclip/FEASIBILITY.md`](./integrations/paperclip/FEASIBILITY.md) — Phase 0 validation report; documents the SPEC errata that surfaced against the SDK at `paperclipai/paperclip@master`.

## Tooling

Once the wiki is set up, you can read and edit pages with any markdown viewer. [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md) is a particularly good fit because of its graph view, `[[wikilinks]]` syntax, and Web Clipper extension, but it isn't required — the wiki is just a directory of markdown files in your project.

The tools require Python 3.10+ and `uv`. Initialization and upgrade invoke `setup_wiki.py`, whose PEP 723 environment pins FastEmbed 0.8.0, sqlite-vec 0.1.9, and PyYAML 6.0.3; it caches the model and synchronizes the complete wiki index. Search, graph lint, and graph extraction also carry their own pinned script metadata. Lexical `wiki_search.py --no-embed`, `wiki_lint.py`, `wiki_stats.py`, and graph queries remain directly runnable with stdlib Python. The bundled scripts live in `skills/llm-wiki/scripts/` after install.

## Credits

The optional skill-evolution workflow is adapted from the [WikiSkill paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.27454v1). The [adaptation map](docs/evolution.md#research-basis-and-adaptation) distinguishes the research ideas, our implementation choices and validation limits.

The pattern is from Andrej Karpathy's [llm-wiki gist](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f), April 2026. This plugin is one implementation of the pattern; others worth looking at include [vanillaflava/llm-wiki-claude-skills](https://github.com/vanillaflava/llm-wiki-claude-skills), [skyllwt/OmegaWiki](https://github.com/skyllwt/OmegaWiki), and [axoviq-ai/synthadoc](https://github.com/axoviq-ai/synthadoc).

The v2 retrieval architecture was informed by Cerebras's engineering article, [How We Built Our Knowledge Base](https://www.cerebras.ai/blog/how-we-built-our-knowledge-base), especially its section-level retrieval, multi-retriever fusion, evidence packaging, and evaluation approach.

The v3 local retrieval cutover was evaluated against [Basic Memory](https://github.com/basicmachines-co/basic-memory). LLM Wiki adopts the same local-first shape—FastEmbed, SQLite vector search, and incremental derived indexes—while keeping its existing Markdown schema, typed graph, RRF ranking, and agent-native workflows instead of adding Basic Memory's application and MCP service as a second canonical system.

## License

MIT — see [LICENSE](./LICENSE).

## Contributing

Issues and PRs welcome. The skill itself is at `skills/llm-wiki/`; the slash commands at `commands/wiki/`. Before opening a PR, please run the bundled scripts against a small test wiki to verify nothing broke.

Global and Local Wikis 161: 162: LLM Wiki Compiler supports two layers: 163: 164: | Layer | Default location | Use it for | 165: | --- | --- | --- | 166: | Global wiki | `~/Knowledge` | Cross-project links, ideas, research, videos, bookmarks, and reusable patterns | 167: | Local wiki | Current repo/folder with `.wiki-compiler.json` | Deep project-specific architecture, decisions, source files, and operating knowledge | 168: 169: The default global folder is: 170: 171: ```text 172: ~/Knowledge 173: ``` 174: 175: You can override it: 176: 177: ```bash 178: export LLM_WIKI_GLOBAL_DIR="$HOME/CompanyKnowledge" 179: ``` 180: 181: Routing defaults: 182: 183: - "capture this in my wiki" → global wiki 184: - "capture this in this repo/project wiki" → local wiki 185: - "capture this in both" → global and local 186: - no global wiki yet → initialize `~/Knowledge` automatically from the global wiki template 187: 188: Set it up explicitly with: 189: 190: ```text 191: Set up my global wiki 192: ``` 193: 194: ## Codebase Mode (New in v2.0) 195: 196: Generate a wiki from a code repository — not just markdown files, but the full knowledge embedded in your codebase: architecture, API contracts, decision records, deployment configs, and gotchas. 197: 198: ### Quick Start 199: 200: ```bash 201: # One command to set up and compile 202: /wiki-init --codebase 203: ``` 204: 205: The compiler auto-detects your project type, discovers modules/services, finds knowledge files (READMEs, ADRs, API specs, Docker configs), and compiles everything into topic articles. 206: 207: ### What It Scans 208: 209: | File Type | Examples | What It Captures | 210: |-----------|----------|-----------------| 211: | Documentation | `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md` | Purpose, architecture, conventions | 212: | API contracts | `*.proto`, `*.graphql`, `openapi.yaml` | API surface, inter-service communication | 213: | Decision records | `ADR-*.md`, `docs/adr/*.md` | Key decisions and rationale | 214: | Infrastructure | `docker-compose.yml`, `Dockerfile`, `k8s/*.yaml` | Deployment topology, scaling | 215: | Operations | `docs/runbooks/*.md`, `CHANGELOG.md` | Gotchas, failure modes, version history | 216: | Config shape | `.env.example`, `package.json` | Environment requirements, dependencies | 217: 218: With `deep_scan: true`, it also reads entry points, type definitions, and route files for richer articles. 219: 220: ### Example Output 221: 222: ```markdown 223: # auth-service 224: 225: ## Purpose [coverage: high -- 8 sources] 226: Handles user authentication and session management via JWT tokens. 227: All other services call auth-service to validate requests. 228: 229: ## Talks To [coverage: high -- 6 sources] 230: - **user-service** (REST: /api/users/:id) -- subscription status lookup 231: - **notification-service** (SQS: auth.password-reset) -- triggers email 232: - **billing-service** (gRPC) -- validates payment status before premium access 233: 234: ## Key Decisions [coverage: medium -- 3 sources] 235: - **JWT over sessions** -- stateless scaling, no shared session store (ADR-003) 236: - **Refresh token rotation** -- security requirement from compliance audit 237: 238: ## Gotchas [coverage: high -- 5 sources] 239: - Token expiry is 15 minutes, not 1 hour (changed in v2.3) 240: - Rate limiting on /auth/login is per-IP, not per-user 241: ``` 242: 243: ### How It Differs from Google Code Wiki / DeepWiki 244: 245: Those tools answer "what does this code do?" by parsing functions and generating API docs. 246: 247: This tool answers **"what does this project *know*?"** by synthesizing documentation, decision records, deployment configs, and operational knowledge into articles an agent can navigate. 248: 249: | | Google Code Wiki / DeepWiki | LLM Wiki Compiler | 250: |---|---|---| 251: | Input | Source code (AST parsing) | Knowledge files + optional code | 252: | Output | API docs + architecture diagrams | Synthesized topic articles with coverage indicators | 253: | Infrastructure | Hosted platform / server + embeddings | Zero infra — Claude Code plugin | 254: | Updates | Full regen on every commit | Incremental — only changed topics | 255: | Consumer | Developers reading docs | Your AI agent (and you) | 256: 257: ### Monorepo / Microservice Support 258: 259: For monorepos, the compiler detects service boundaries by looking for directories with their own manifest files (`package.json`, `go.mod`, etc.). Each service becomes a topic article. Cross-cutting concerns (infrastructure, testing, deployment) get their own articles. 260: 261: ``` 262: 📚 Wiki compiled — 8 topics from 47 files 263: 264: Topics created: 265: ├── auth-service (12 sources) 266: ├── billing-service (9 sources) 267: ├── notification-service (6 sources) 268: ├── api-gateway (5 sources) 269: ├── infrastructure (4 sources) 270: ├── testing (3 sources) 271: └── deployment (3 sources) 272: 273: Concepts discovered: 274: ├── error-handling-strategy — shared pattern across 4 services 275: └── auth-flow — touches auth, gateway, billing 276: ``` 277: 278: ### Codebase Configuration 279: 280: ```json 281: { 282: "version": 2, 283: "mode": "codebase", 284: "name": "My Project", 285: "sources": [{ "path": "./", "exclude": ["node_modules/", "dist/", ".git/", "wiki/"] }], 286: "output": "wiki/", 287: "service_discovery": "auto", 288: "deep_scan": false, 289: "knowledge_files": ["README.md", "CLAUDE.md", "*.proto", "openapi.*", "ADR-*.md", "Dockerfile"] 290: } 291: ``` 292: 293: | Field | Description | 294: |-------|-------------| 295: | `mode` | `"codebase"` enables code-aware topic discovery | 296: | `service_discovery` | `"auto"` detects monorepo vs single project | 297: | `deep_scan` | `true` to also read source code files for richer articles | 298: | `knowledge_files` | Glob patterns for priority documentation files | 299: 300: ## Knowledge Graph Visualization 301: 302: See your compiled wiki as an interactive knowledge graph. Topics appear as nodes sized by source count, concepts as connecting edges. 303: 304: ```bash 305: /wiki-visualize 306: ``` 307: 308: - **Hover** nodes to see source count and highlight connections 309: - **Click** a node to read the full article in a side panel with coverage badges 310: - **Shift-click** a node to expand its neighborhood — concept-connected topics light up, others dim. Shift-click again to keep walking the graph (depth 2, depth 3, …). The HUD shows how many nodes and seeds are currently lit. 311: - **Hover edges** to see concept names linking topics 312: - **Search** to filter topics by name or alias 313: - **Escape** to close the article panel or clear the expansion 314: 315: Canvas-based, zero dependencies, Nothing Design System tokens (Space Grotesk + Space Mono typography). Works with both knowledge mode and codebase mode wikis. 316: 317: You can also run it manually without the plugin: 318: ```bash 319: node plugin/visualize/server.js --wiki-dir path/to/wiki/ 320: # Open http://localhost:3848 321: ``` 322: 323: ## Fetch from External Sources 324: 325: Your context isn't always on disk — a lot of it lives in services like X bookmarks, Readwise highlights, or Pocket saves. `/fetch-bookmarks ` pulls that content into a local directory that `/wiki-compile` can consume alongside your regular sources. 326: 327: Optional — skip it entirely if all your sources are already local markdown. 328: 329: ### Quick Start 330: 331: ```bash 332: /fetch-bookmarks x 333: ``` 334: 335: First run walks you through: 336: 337: 1. Checking that Node.js 20+ is installed 338: 2. Installing [Field Theory CLI](https://github.com/afar1/fieldtheory-cli) (MIT-licensed, free) globally via npm — one consent prompt 339: 3. Syncing your X bookmarks using Chrome cookie auth (no X API key needed) 340: 4. Adding `~/.ft-bookmarks/md/` to your `.wiki-compiler.json` sources 341: 342: After that, `/fetch-bookmarks x` just resyncs. Run `/wiki-compile` whenever you want bookmarks folded into topic articles. 343: 344: ### Auto-Sync (Set and Forget) 345: 346: Manual syncing gets forgotten. Install a daily background job: 347: 348: ```bash 349: /fetch-bookmarks schedule x 350: ``` 351: 352: On macOS this writes a `launchd` plist to `~/Library/LaunchAgents/dev.llm-wiki-compiler.x-sync.plist` that runs `ft sync && ft md` daily at 03:00 local. No LLM tokens, no Claude Code needed — pure shell. On Linux/WSL you get a `crontab` snippet to paste. 353: 354: The `/wiki-compile` step stays manual by design — it needs an LLM and your judgment. When you next open Claude Code in a wiki project, the session-start hook tells you how many new bookmarks have arrived since the last compile, so your intent translates to action without you having to track dates. 355: 356: Uninstall with `/fetch-bookmarks schedule x --uninstall` (or `launchctl unload` manually). 357: 358: ### Available Sources 359: 360: | Source | Status | Backend | 361: |--------|--------|---------| 362: | `x` | Shipped | [Field Theory CLI](https://github.com/afar1/fieldtheory-cli) (MIT) | 363: | `readwise` | Planned | TBD | 364: | `pocket` | Planned | TBD | 365: | `github-stars` | Planned | TBD | 366: 367: ### How It Works 368: 369: `/fetch-bookmarks` is a thin dispatcher. Each source has its own adapter at `plugin/skills/wiki-compiler/adapters/.md` that handles dependency checks, auth, sync, and wiring the output directory into your wiki config. Adapters delegate to existing open-source tools rather than reimplementing fetch logic — so you get a stable plugin surface (`/fetch-bookmarks x`) while the heavy lifting is maintained upstream. 370: 371: ### Requirements 372: 373: - **Node.js 20+** (for Field Theory CLI) 374: - **Chrome** (for first-time X cookie sync — this is a Field Theory CLI limitation) 375: 376: ### Contributing a New Adapter 377: 378: Copy `plugin/skills/wiki-compiler/adapters/x.md` and follow the contract documented in `plugin/commands/fetch-bookmarks.md`: preflight, consent, sync, markdown output, wire into `sources[]`, suggest compile. 379: 380: ## Capture Links With Context 381: 382: The primary UX is: paste a link and say **"capture this in my wiki."** You do not need to remember command names. 383: 384: In Codex: 385: 386: ```text 387: https://example.com/article 388: 389: capture this in my wiki 390: ``` 391: 392: Add context when you have it: 393: 394: ```text 395: https://example.com/article 396: 397: capture this in my wiki 398: 399: Context: Relevant to Codex plugin onboarding and skill discovery. 400: ``` 401: 402: Claude Code users can use the explicit command form: 403: 404: ```bash 405: /wiki-capture https://example.com/article --context "Relevant to Codex plugin onboarding and skill discovery" 406: ``` 407: 408: The capture flow is adapter-based: 409: 410: | Source | Adapter | What gets saved | 411: |--------|---------|-----------------| 412: | Web article | `capture-web` | readable page text, metadata, relevance notes | 413: | YouTube | `capture-youtube` | transcript evidence, timestamps, workflow notes when relevant | 414: | X/Twitter link | `capture-x` | post/thread text or bookmark source, date-aware relevance notes | 415: 416: Captured links are written to `wiki-sources/captures/` inside the target wiki as markdown with frontmatter, the original URL, captured date, user context, extracted content, relevance notes, and candidate wiki connections. The wiki then uses the same ingest/compile logic to update existing topics or propose a new topic/concept. 417: 418: ### Connector Roadmap 419: 420: The capture system is intentionally adapter-based. Future connectors should feed durable, provenance-rich source markdown into the same compiler pipeline instead of writing topic articles directly. 421: 422: Planned connector shape: 423: 424: ```text 425: connector pulls context 426: → normalizes to markdown with metadata 427: → writes to wiki-sources/{connector}/ 428: → adds that folder to sources[] 429: → wiki compile builds topic/concept connections 430: ``` 431: 432: Candidate connectors: 433: 434: | Connector | Use case | 435: |-----------|----------| 436: | Granola | Meeting notes, summaries, decisions, and follow-ups | 437: | Google Drive / Docs | Docs, strategy notes, specs, and research folders | 438: | Slack | High-signal threads, decisions, and customer/team context | 439: | Linear / GitHub Issues | Roadmap, bugs, project decisions, and implementation context | 440: | Readwise / Pocket | Reading highlights and saved articles | 441: 442: The key rule: connectors create source material; the wiki compiler owns synthesis and connections. 443: 444: ## How It Works (Knowledge Mode) 445: 446: ### Commands 447: 448: | Command | Purpose | 449: |---------|---------| 450: | `/wiki-init` | One-time setup -- auto-detects markdown directories, samples files, proposes custom article structure | 451: | `/wiki-global-init` | Initialize the default global wiki at `~/Knowledge` or `LLM_WIKI_GLOBAL_DIR` | 452: | `/wiki-compile` | Compiles source files into topic articles (incremental -- only recompiles changes). Generates `schema.md` on first run. | 453: | `/wiki-capture` | Capture a URL plus context, normalize it into markdown, and connect it to existing topics/concepts | 454: | `/wiki-ingest` | Add a single source interactively -- read, discuss key takeaways, update relevant wiki articles | 455: | `/fetch-bookmarks` | Pull bookmarks from external services (X today; Readwise, Pocket planned). `schedule ` wires a daily launchd job. | 456: | `/wiki-search` | Search across wiki articles by keyword or phrase | 457: | `/wiki-lint` | Health checks -- finds stale articles, orphan pages, missing cross-references, contradictions, low coverage | 458: | `/wiki-query` | Optional -- Q&A against the wiki. Can file useful answers back into wiki articles. | 459: | `/wiki-migrate` | One-time migration -- analyzes your AGENTS.md startup reads, shows which are covered by wiki, generates replacement | 460: | `/wiki-visualize` | Launch interactive knowledge graph of your compiled wiki | 461: | `/wiki-upgrade` | Update the plugin to the latest version from GitHub | 462: 463: The primary workflow is: **init → compile → add to AGENTS.md → done.** After that, Claude reads the wiki automatically. `/wiki-query` is a convenience for testing or quick lookups. 464: 465: ### Staged Adoption (The Key Feature) 466: 467: The plugin never modifies your existing CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md. Instead, it injects context via a SessionStart hook with three modes: 468: 469: | Mode | What Happens | Your Existing Setup | 470: |------|-------------|-------------------| 471: | **staging** (default) | "Wiki available — check it when you need depth" | Completely unchanged | 472: | **recommended** | "Check wiki articles before raw files" | Unchanged, but Claude prioritizes wiki | 473: | **primary** | "Wiki is your primary knowledge source" | You can optionally simplify startup reads | 474: 475: Change mode by editing `.wiki-compiler.json`: 476: ```json 477: { "mode": "staging" } → { "mode": "recommended" } → { "mode": "primary" } 478: ``` 479: 480: ### What Gets Compiled 481: 482: During `/wiki-init`, the compiler samples your source files and proposes an article structure that fits your domain. You approve (or tweak) the sections before anything gets compiled. 483: 484: For example, a product team's wiki might get: 485: - **Summary** — **Timeline** — **Current State** — **Key Decisions** — **Experiments & Results** — **Gotchas** — **Open Questions** — **Sources** 486: 487: While a research wiki might get: 488: - **Summary** — **Key Findings** — **Methodology** — **Evidence** — **Gaps & Contradictions** — **Open Questions** — **Sources** 489: 490: And a book notes wiki might get: 491: - **Summary** — **Characters** — **Themes** — **Plot Threads** — **Connections** — **Quotes** — **Sources** 492: 493: The structure is saved in `.wiki-compiler.json` and can be edited anytime. **Summary** and **Sources** are always included. 494: 495: ### Coverage Indicators (Best of Both Worlds) 496: 497: Every section includes a coverage tag so you (or your AI agent) know when to trust the wiki vs when to read raw sources: 498: 499: ```markdown 500: ## Summary [coverage: high -- 15 sources] 501: ...trust this, it's well-sourced... 502: 503: ## Experiments & Results [coverage: medium -- 3 sources] 504: ...decent overview, check raw files for details... 505: 506: ## Gotchas [coverage: low -- 1 source] 507: ...read the raw gotchas.md directly... 508: ``` 509: 510: - **high** (5+ sources) — trust the wiki section directly 511: - **medium** (2-4 sources) — good overview, check raw sources for granular questions 512: - **low** (0-1 sources) — read the raw sources listed in that section 513: 514: This gives you the speed of the wiki (84% fewer tokens) without sacrificing accuracy. Your agent reads the wiki first, and only falls back to raw files for low-coverage sections. 515: 516: ### Time-Decay Awareness 517: 518: Tweets from 2022 and tweets from 2026 don't carry equal weight on questions about AI tooling or UI patterns — so the compiler doesn't treat them as equal either. For **time-sensitive topics** (AI, design, growth tactics, bookmark-heavy topics), the compiler: 519: 520: - Extracts a source date from each input (frontmatter `posted_at` / `date`, filename date, or mtime) 521: - Orders Timeline and Key Decisions bullets newest-first, date-prefixed 522: - Flags claims older than 18 months with ⚠️ 523: - Adds `[as of YYYY-MM]` tags to sections resting mostly on aging sources 524: - In conflicts, prefers the newer source and notes the shift 525: 526: Stable topics (career, personal growth, visa work) use looser thresholds (24/48 months). Nothing gets deleted — stale entries stay for historical context, just clearly marked. 527: 528: ### Obsidian Compatible 529: 530: The wiki output is plain markdown with Obsidian-style `[[wikilinks]]`. Open `wiki/INDEX.md` in Obsidian and you'll see the full knowledge base with bidirectional links to source files. 531: 532: ### Concept Articles (Cross-Cutting Patterns) 533: 534: After compiling topic articles, the compiler looks for patterns that span 3+ topics and generates **concept articles** in `wiki/concepts/`. These are interpretive, not just factual -- they answer "what does this pattern mean?" not just "what happened?" 535: 536: Examples from a real project: 537: - **"Speed vs Quality Tradeoff"** -- 6 instances where this decision appeared across retention, push notifications, and experiment design 538: - **"Cross-Team Decision Patterns"** -- communication patterns and decision dynamics synthesized from 24 meetings 539: - **"Evolution of Retention Thinking"** -- how the approach changed from Oct 2025 to Apr 2026 across analytics, strategy, and experiments 540: 541: Concept articles are discovered automatically during compilation. You can also seed them in `schema.md` if you know what patterns you want tracked. 542: 543: ### Schema Document 544: 545: On first compile, a `schema.md` is generated in your wiki output directory. It defines your wiki's structure: topic list, naming conventions, article format, and cross-reference rules. 546: 547: You can edit `schema.md` to rename topics, merge them, or add conventions. The compiler reads it before each run and respects your changes. New topics get added automatically with an evolution log entry. 548: 549: ### Wiki Lint 550: 551: Run `/wiki-lint` to check wiki health: 552: 553: - **Stale articles** -- sources changed since last compile 554: - **Orphan pages** -- articles with deleted/missing sources 555: - **Missing cross-references** -- topics sharing 3+ sources that don't link to each other 556: - **Low coverage sections** -- `[coverage: low]` tags flagged for improvement 557: - **Contradictions** -- conflicting facts across articles (e.g., different dates for same event) 558: - **Schema drift** -- topics in wiki/ not listed in schema.md, or vice versa 559: 560: ### Query Filing 561: 562: When `/wiki-query` produces a useful synthesis that connects information across topics, it offers to file the answer back into the relevant wiki article. Your explorations compound in the knowledge base instead of disappearing with the session. 563: 564: ## Configuration 565: 566: `.wiki-compiler.json` (created by `/wiki-init`): 567: 568: ```json 569: { 570: "version": 2, 571: "name": "My Project", 572: "mode": "staging", 573: "sources": [ 574: { "path": "Knowledge/", "exclude": ["wiki/"] }, 575: { "path": "docs/meetings/" } 576: ], 577: "output": "Knowledge/wiki/", 578: "topic_hints": ["retention", "onboarding"], 579: "link_style": "obsidian" 580: } 581: ``` 582: 583: | Field | Description | 584: |-------|-------------| 585: | `version` | Config version (`2` for latest) | 586: | `name` | Display name for the knowledge base | 587: | `mode` | Integration mode: `staging` / `recommended` / `primary` — OR `codebase` for code repositories | 588: | `sources` | Directories to scan | 589: | `output` | Where compiled wiki lives | 590: | `article_sections` | Article structure — generated during `/wiki-init` based on your content (see below) | 591: | `topic_hints` | Optional seed topics to guide classification | 592: | `link_style` | `obsidian` (wikilinks) or `markdown` (standard links) | 593: | `service_discovery` | (codebase mode) `auto` or `manual` — how to detect modules/services | 594: | `knowledge_files` | (codebase mode) Glob patterns for priority documentation files | 595: | `deep_scan` | (codebase mode) `true` to also read source code files | 596: 597: ### Custom Article Structure 598: 599: The `article_sections` array defines what sections appear in each topic article. It's generated during `/wiki-init` by sampling your source files — the compiler proposes sections that fit your domain, and you approve or tweak them. 600: 601: ```json 602: "article_sections": [ 603: { "name": "Summary", "description": "standalone briefing of the topic", "required": true }, 604: { "name": "Key Findings", "description": "main discoveries and insights" }, 605: { "name": "Methodology", "description": "approaches and methods used" }, 606: { "name": "Open Questions", "description": "unresolved threads and gaps" }, 607: { "name": "Sources", "description": "backlinks to all contributing files", "required": true } 608: ] 609: ``` 610: 611: You can edit this array anytime — add, remove, or rename sections. The compiler will use your updated structure on the next `/wiki-compile` run. `Summary` and `Sources` are required and cannot be removed. 612: 613: If `article_sections` is missing (older configs), the compiler falls back to a default template. 614: 615: ## Safety Guarantees 616: 617: - Source files are **never modified** — the compiler only writes to the output directory 618: - The wiki can be **deleted and regenerated** at any time from source files 619: - Your **CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md are never touched** — context injection happens via hooks 620: - **Rollback anytime** — change mode back to `staging` or delete `.wiki-compiler.json` 621: 622: ## Cost Savings (Real Data) 623: 624: Tested on a real project with 1,183 markdown files across meetings, strategy docs, session histories, and research notes. 625: 626: ### Token Reduction 627: 628: | | Without Wiki | With Wiki | 629: |---|---|---| 630: | Session startup context | ~79K tokens (13 files) | ~8.5K tokens (INDEX + 2-3 articles) | 631: | Per-question research | ~8,000 tokens (10+ files) | ~600 tokens (1 article) | 632: | **Reduction** | — | **89%** | 633: 634: ### Compilation Costs 635: 636: | | Tokens | Cost (Opus) | Cost (Sonnet) | 637: |---|---|---|---| 638: | First compilation | ~880K | ~$13 | ~$2.60 | 639: | Daily incremental | ~100K | ~$1.50 | ~$0.30 | 640: | **Break-even** | — | **First session** | **First session** | 641: 642: ### Accuracy 643: 644: We spot-checked wiki articles against their raw source files: 645: 646: - **10/10 key facts accurately synthesized** -- no fabrication, no missing critical details 647: - **Coverage indicators are honest** -- sections marked `[coverage: high]` had 5+ contributing sources 648: - **Trade-off is transparent** -- wiki captures ~90% of raw file content; coverage tags tell you when to fall back to raw sources for the remaining 10% 649: 650: ### Compression 651: 652: - 1,183 files → 14 topic articles -- **84x compression** 653: - Session startup: 13 file reads → 1 INDEX + 2-3 topic articles -- **89% fewer tokens** 654: - ~$1.05 saved per session at Opus pricing ($15/M input tokens) 655: 656: ## Integrating with AGENTS.md (Recommended) 657: 658: This is the main way to use the wiki long-term. After you've compiled and spot-checked the output, add this to your project's AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md: 659: 660: ```markdown 661: ## Knowledge Base 662: 663: A compiled knowledge wiki is available at `{your output path}/`. 664: 665: **Session startup:** Read `wiki/INDEX.md` for a topic overview, then read 666: specific topic articles relevant to your current task. 667: 668: **Using coverage indicators:** Each section has a coverage tag: 669: - `[coverage: high]` -- trust this section, skip the raw files. 670: - `[coverage: medium]` -- good overview, check raw sources for granular questions. 671: - `[coverage: low]` -- read the raw sources listed in that section directly. 672: 673: **When you need depth:** Check the article's Sources section for links to 674: raw files. Only read raw sources for medium/low coverage sections or when 675: you need very specific detail. 676: 677: **Never modify wiki files directly** -- they are regenerated by `/wiki-compile`. 678: ``` 679: 680: Once this is in your AGENTS.md, Claude automatically uses the wiki every session with smart fallback. High-coverage sections save tokens. Low-coverage sections point Claude to the exact raw files it needs. 681: 682: **When to add this:** After running `/wiki-compile` at least once and validating that the topic articles accurately reflect your knowledge. 683: 684: ## Advanced 685: 686: ### Incremental Compilation 687: 688: After the first full compile, `/wiki-compile` only recompiles topics whose source files changed. INDEX.md is always regenerated. 689: 690: ### Force Full Recompile 691: 692: ``` 693: /wiki-compile --full 694: ``` 695: 696: ### Compile Single Topic 697: 698: ``` 699: /wiki-compile --topic retention 700: ``` 701: 702: ### Interactive Ingest 703: 704: Add sources one at a time with `/wiki-ingest`: 705: 706: ``` 707: /wiki-ingest path/to/new-meeting-notes.md 708: ``` 709: 710: The compiler reads the file, shows you key takeaways, asks what to emphasize, then updates all relevant topic articles. Results include coverage indicators so you know when to trust the wiki vs read raw sources. 723: 724: For synthesis questions that require connecting multiple topics, use `/wiki-query` instead. 725: 726: For large wikis (100+ topics), consider adding [qmd](https://github.com/jina-ai/qmd) as an MCP server for hybrid BM25/vector search with LLM re-ranking. 727: 728: ### Migrate to Wiki-First Startup 729: 730: Once your wiki is compiled and spot-checked, run `/wiki-migrate` to switch your AGENTS.md from reading raw files to reading the wiki: 731: 732: ``` 733: /wiki-migrate 734: 735: Wiki Migration Report for "My Project" 736: 737: Current startup: 13 file reads 738: 739: ✅ gotchas.md → covered by analytics [coverage: high] 740: ✅ product-context.md → covered by product [coverage: high] 741: ⚠️ reporting-backlog.md → partially covered [coverage: medium] 742: ❌ acceptance-criteria.md → not covered (operational checklist) 743: 744: Summary: 10/13 reads can be replaced 745: Estimated savings: ~79K → ~8.5K tokens (89% reduction) 746: ``` 747: 748: The command generates a replacement startup section and applies it with your confirmation. 749: 750: ### Stale Wiki Detection 751: 752: The plugin automatically detects when source files have changed since the last compile.
